analysis.one_liner: Bars tax-exempt "social welfare" groups from spending more than 10% of their money on politics and makes them reveal donors of $5,000 or more.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote: after its November 2021 introduction it sat in the House Ways and Means Committee until the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Groups organized as 501(c)(4) "social welfare" organizations do not have to name their donors, which is why they are the main vehicle for "dark money" — political advertising that voters cannot trace to its funders. This bill would have changed that in two ways: it would have stripped a 501(c)(4) of its tax exemption if more than 10% of its spending went to political activity, and it would have forced any 501(c)(4) that spends on politics to publicly disclose the name and address of every contributor giving $5,000 or more. The bill never advanced past a committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters would benefit most directly: any group paying for election ads or mailers through a "social welfare" shell would have to reveal who funded them, so people watching a political commercial could find out who paid for it. Candidates and parties would also benefit in a limited way, because groups that currently operate outside campaign-finance disclosure would lose their tax exemption if they spent more than 10% of their budget on politics, pushing that spending back into channels with public reporting.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters who want to trace political ads

how_it_helps.text: A social welfare organization that spends money on politics would have to publicly disclose the name and address of every contributor giving $5,000 or more, letting voters see who is bankrolling the ads and mailers that try to sway their votes.

By stripping tax-exempt status from any 501(c)(4) spending more than 10% of its budget on political activity — with a broad definition of 'political intervention' covering express advocacy, electioneering communications, and transfers of resources for campaigns — the bill would have made it much less attractive to park campaign money in a 'social welfare' shell.

The bill directed the Treasury Secretary to write regulations preventing avoidance, including rules covering transfers of assets to entities controlled by the same people, aimed at stopping groups from simply renaming or restructuring to escape the limits.

analysis.who_pays: Tax-exempt 501(c)(4) organizations that engage in politics, and the wealthy donors who fund them anonymously, would bear the cost: they would either cap political spending, disclose their donors, or lose their tax exemption. Issue-advocacy groups generally would face new compliance burdens from the bill's broad definition of "political intervention," and political advertisers would lose business if dark-money spending dried up.
analysis.who_pays_short: Tax-exempt political groups and their donors

drawbacks.text: The bill would have required public disclosure of the name and address of anyone giving $5,000 or more to a 501(c)(4) that spends on politics, which donor-privacy advocates have long argued exposes contributors to harassment, boycotts, or retaliation — a burden that falls on donors of every political persuasion.

The new 'political intervention' definition sweeps in not just express advocacy but any communication that refers to a candidate and reflects a view on them, plus 'political use of resources' — a broad net that civic groups, community organizations, and unions' social-welfare arms would have to navigate, with real risk of chill on ordinary issue advocacy.

The 10% cap and disclosure apply only to 501(c)(4) social welfare organizations; other channels for political money, such as super PACs (which already disclose) and certain other tax-exempt entities, are not addressed by this bill, so the dark-money problem would be narrowed rather than eliminated.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real: a small number of very large donors would no longer be able to shape elections invisibly through tax-exempt groups, and voters would know who was paying for the political ads they see. The costs are also real: the same disclosure could expose donors of any political persuasion to harassment, and the 10% cap plus a broad definition of "political intervention" would force civic and issue groups to steer clear of politics in election years or reorganize. The bill was a fairly blunt instrument and offered no carve-outs for small or low-budget groups. On balance it targeted a genuine gap — billions in undisclosed election spending — with a mechanism that worked but had real side effects worth tightening. Its larger flaw was political: it never got a hearing, so its design was never tested or improved.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, so it died silently when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: H.R. 5997 was introduced in the House on November 17, 2021 by Rep. Jared Golden with three Democratic cosponsors.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means — the committee that handles changes to the tax code — and that referral was the last action of any kind.
The committee never held a hearing or markup, the House never debated the bill, and no vote was ever taken before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, at which point the bill expired.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tax-exempt political organizations and their large anonymous donors, who can continue spending undisclosed money on elections; voters never gained the disclosure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Anonymous donors and the groups that shield them

for.name: Rep. Jared Golden
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Crack Down on Dark Money Act on November 17, 2021.

for.name: Reps. Val Demings, Eleanor Holmes Norton, and Mark DeSaulnier
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsors of the bill; the only members to sign on.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: The committee that handles all tax-code changes never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; the record shows no action after the November 17, 2021 referral.

against.name: House Republican conference
against.what_they_did: No Republican member signed on as a cosponsor, and the bill never attracted bipartisan support that could have moved it.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the partisan split never got tested on the floor; the sponsor and all three cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican signed on.

industries.note: Groups using social-welfare status as a channel for campaign spending would have lost their tax exemption above a 10% political-spending cap and had to name their large donors. This is the bill's direct target: the organizations through which undisclosed money moves into elections.

Donors giving $5,000 or more to politically active 501(c)(4)s would have been publicly identified, ending the ability to fund election ads anonymously. Ordinary voters would see who was paying for the political messaging aimed at them.

Less dark money flowing through 501(c)(4)s would mean fewer untraceable ads, mailers, and robocalls purchased around elections. For viewers, fewer anonymous political ads; for the ad industry, some revenue.

Most 501(c)(4)s that stay out of elections would be unaffected, but mixed-purpose groups would face compliance burdens, and the broad 'political intervention' definition could sweep in routine advocacy that mentions a candidate during an election season.
